tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description: Publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit (some clients refuse any artifact but your own as owner-only), by replacing text in its current document: use it for a small change instead of sending the whole page to publish_version. The server reads the live index.html, applies every edit in order, and publishes the result as one new version; if any edit cannot be applied, nothing is published. Each old_text must occur exactly once in the document as it stands when that edit is applied: include enough surrounding text to make it unique. base_version must name the live version (from get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result); if it is no longer live the call is rejected with a conflict that names the live version: read what you are changing again and retry. To rename the artifact pass title, which also rewrites the document's <title> element; an edit to that element without title is refused, because the server keeps it in step with the artifact's title. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document cannot be edited here. An artifact made from a type is edited only if this server offers list_files, and only with path: one of its own text files, as list_files lists them, never its page or its type's files.

## claude-artifacts
Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.

  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If

  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.

Desktop Commander provides tools for working with the user's authorized device.

160	**Conventions.** Rules are `LO-n` (the prefix is free in every sibling GDD). Formulas are referred to by their registry names (`soft_pool_scale`, `hard_cone_scale`, `modifier_stack`, `flash_governor`, `ambient_value`, `hull_floor`, `shadow_slot_assign`, `cut_order`, `lod_tier`, `per_rung_lit_pixels`, `texture_magnification`, `warmup_ramp`, `glow_threshold_bound`, `light_energy_from_pm`, `gutter_recipe`, `flare_flicker`, `decoy_budget`, `edge_width_screen_px`, `beam_offset`); the Formulas section assigns their `D.n`, and every formula that is not this GDD's is qualified (`EM D.7`, `Graph D.6`, `PIPE D.5`, `PC D.12`, `kernel D.10`). Every engine statement carries `[REF]` (verified from `docs/engine-reference/godot/`), `[BIN]` (existence, type or default only, from the installed 4.7.2 class dump in ART 8.4/8.10) or `[UNV]` (unverified; the named spike step settles it, ART 8.12). Every number this GDD introduces is a placeholder, owner technical-artist, "confirmed by the Lighting spike step n"; every borrowed number is used by its registry name and value and is never restated differently (a needed different value is a CONFLICT surfaced in Open Questions, never a silent change). Rule text is behaviour; where an implementation choice would be needed it is a "-> ADR candidate" note. Zoom-dependent statements hold at **every** rung `k_z` in [1, `k_auto` + 2] and under **both** render passes (PIPE PR-7), on 1080p (`k_auto` 3), 1440p (`k_auto` 4), the Deck (1280x800, `expand`, `k_auto` 2) and 2160p (`k_auto` 6), not only at the default zoom.
161	
162	**LO-1. Rendering only; Lighting reads, the simulation never reads Lighting.** Lighting is a `PRESENTATION` subscriber (KERN:108-113). It reads the last-committed `SIM` views (`emitter.state` and its `shapes()` table, Layout's `OccluderSource`) and, for decoys and module-body glows only, `PERCEPTION_OUT` lists; its notification handlers only mark dirty (kernel CR-10: handler = dirty mark only, writes disabled in handlers) and all drawing happens in the LIGHTING stage's present step of the PresentationDriver (ADR-0009 § 3; stage 6, after AVATAR and FILTER, so the Presenter's beam pose and the decoy list are already written) *(Amended 2026-10-29 — ADR-0009 sync)*. It writes only `CanvasItem`, `Material`, `Light2D`, `LightOccluder2D` and `CanvasModulate` properties, all inside layer 0 of the world viewport that the Pipeline owns. It owns no simulation fact, no reach, no output, no `lit`; it never writes an emitter, never reports a cull to the simulation (a sim-lit but unrendered light would be a P1 lie, so the answer to over-budget is demotion, LO-23, not silence), and registers **no state block, no step hook and no `after:` entry**. Hook ids appear in this document only as things Lighting does *not* order against (`emitter.place`, `body.integrate`) and never in an example. The occluder builder (LO-11) is the one derived-object duty and is classed `PROJECTOR` (KERN:112); the kernel marks that reading provisional pending a technical-director ruling (KERN:117, Open Question 1) and this GDD does not pre-empt it (-> ADR candidate: occluder projector class). The test for ownership (mirroring Emitter State guard G1): if a sentence needs a `Light2D` to be true it belongs here, otherwise it belongs to the owner and is cited by name.

The Perception Filter writes **no** `Light2D` member of any kind. The tool layer carries no light, and no `Light2D` is a child of, or positioned by, the tool layer (hands-free chest lamp, LO-28). The beam node's parent is a non-rotating body-frame node, so that a rotated `offset` is never composed with an avatar rotation (lint). The earlier claim that the two writers "have nothing to race over" remains true, but the dependency is real; if the Presenter's rotation changed after Lighting's `offset` write the apex would be off by up to `|chest − foot| × sin(Δθ)` (1.7 px for PC-5's accepted 2.8 degrees), which the apex-equals-chest lint (≤ 0.01 px every render frame) catches. -> ADR candidate: presentation frame order (a single presentation driver calling Presenter, Lighting, Filter, diagnostics in a fixed order, rather than per-system `process_priority`).
165	
166	**LO-3. Work runs at three cadences: **per committed tick** (a change in the read view's `tick`, observed at the LIGHTING present step): the active set, slot assignment, demotion order, LOD tier, ambient value, occluder sync, using committed inputs only; **per render frame**: pose of moving lights, the modifier chain value, the governor, envelopes, the apply step; **on event**: camera cut, a rung change, a window or pass change, a restore, `LOADING`/`TRANSIT_HOLD` exit, a settings change, the `ALL` dirty collapse (more than `MAX_DIRTY_KEYS` keys). Dirty keys are an optimisation hint only: a full reconcile of every record runs on every event and every `FULL_RECONCILE_TICKS` (placeholder 60), and the incremental result must equal the full result (debug assertion); correctness never depends on a notification arriving. **Determinism, split in two *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*.** (1) *Tick-only decisions* — which emitters are active, slot assignment and lending, demotion order, seat protection, the LOD tier T, the tell tier read, the ambient target, bound or stand-in status — are pure functions of the committed read-view snapshot, the committed camera field, the per-client settings and the previous tick's decision, and are **replay-identical**: a replay and a live run produce identical bindings and identical demotion order. (2) *Envelope and governor outcomes* — the modifier-chain value, the warm-up, cut and shadow fades, gutter onset times, the governor's retiming and every member value that carries them — also depend on `present_time` and the render rate, so they are **deterministic given a recorded frame-time trace** (the `present_time` at every LIGHTING present step), not replay-identical across machines or frame rates. **The plan step / apply step seam and an injectable clock are requirements of this GDD, not ADR candidates:** the plan is computed headlessly, a separate apply step alone names `Light2D`, and the clock is injected so every test supplies its frame-time trace (the testability seam the coding standard asks for). **Fixed pool:** Lighting instantiates a fixed pool of lights, stand-ins, decoy sprites and occluder objects at boot (**`LIGHT_NODE_POOL` = `NONSHADOW_LIGHTS_MAX` 24 + `MAX_FAULT_GLOW` 10 + `LIGHTS_PER_ITEM_MAX` 12 + `SHADOW_SLOTS_MAX` 6 + `n_beam_seats` (the never-demoted `BEAM_SPILL` foot pools, LO-35) = 53 at the single-player MVP and 56 at VS-B**, the non-shadow cap plus the protected excess that may exceed it (fault glows and the seat-protected set, LO-23) plus the shadow casters, asserted at startup against the engine's light and shadow limits read back `[UNV]`; the occluder pool is `OCCLUDER_NODE_POOL`, LO-11) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*; nothing is created or freed during play; a bound emitter keeps its node while eligible (sticky binding, so reordering the demotion list does not rebind lights); every member write is skipped when its value is unchanged (write-on-change). **First observation is never a transition (EP-15):** the first time a light is observed after boot, a restore, a hold exit, a camera cut, a body or pool re-bind, it enters STEADY at its L0 value with no warm-up, no fade and no governor history; warm-up fires only on an observed `output_pm` change from 0 to non-zero between two consecutive committed ticks. **Active set:** an emitter is active iff its reach circle intersects the committed field rectangle expanded by `VIEW_MARGIN_PX` (`VIEW_MARGIN_PX`, placeholder 24 px: the minimum margin is `V_RUN` 3 px per tick × `MAX_TICKS_PER_FRAME` 4 = 12 px of camera travel between committed evaluations, and the placeholder keeps a 2× allowance for camera look-ahead, confirmed at spike step 3, so a light scrolling into view already exists); the test is integer-only so the set is reproducible. A read-view path that does not allocate per poll (struct-of-arrays columns or a caller-provided buffer, plus a monotone `tick` stamp on the view) is asked of Emitter State as Ask E-F (-> ADR candidate), and "newest light" is defined as the **higher emitter id** (ids are monotone, EM-28; Ask E-G confirms), which is reproducible after a restore.

222	**LO-10. Shadow origin: where the engine's shadow starts versus where the simulation's segment starts (a spike-decided conditional; ruled R7).** The simulation's occlusion segment starts at the **foot** (`body.state` `pos_curr`, `beam_pose` `occ_origin`; Ship Body `body.state`, registered `body_state_block`, a SIM read view readable by PRESENTATION), while the cone's apex and reach start at the chest (`chest_point`, `|x| ≤ 2`, y −45 to −25; EM-6). Preference order **B, then A, then D; C rejected on budget.** **Outcome B (preferred):** if spike step 3 verifies that `PointLight2D.offset` `[UNV]` moves the texture apex without moving the shadow origin, the beam node sits at the foot and Lighting writes `offset` so that the apex lands on the floored chest point; because the node rotates with raw aim, `offset` is **not a constant**: it is recomputed every render frame from the rotation the Presenter wrote that frame (`beam_offset`: `Rot(−θ)·v − a_tex` if `offset` is node-local, `v − Rot(θ)·a_tex` if world-fixed, where `v` is the foot-to-chest vector and `a_tex` the texture apex's displacement from the texture centre; spike step 3b reports which frame applies, knob `OFFSET_FRAME`). **Outcome A:** otherwise the node sits at the chest (`beam_offset` then reduces to the texture's own apex term, non-zero by default under the edge-apex layout of LO-15), shadows originate at the chest, and the discrepancy is recorded as AC-57 band: with the player 10-34 px south of a wall the chest can lie inside the wall footprint while the feet do not, and the engine's behaviour for a light inside a closed occluder is `[UNV]` (all-around shadow, or none). **Outcome D** (the simulation occludes from the chest with a wall walk-back, Emitter State ADR candidate 5) is an Emitter State change and is never made here. **Outcome C** (two lights per beam, a cone at the chest plus a shadow-only caster at the foot) is rejected: four beams become eight lights against `SHADOW_SLOTS_MAX`. The member assignment per outcome is LO-2's.
223	
224	**LO-11. The builder creates and updates `LightOccluder2D` nodes `[BIN]` that **it owns** (never occluder layers of a `TileSet` on Layout's or the Pipeline's tilemaps: `occluder_light_mask`, the per-body masks of LO-24 and the lend are per-node properties, and a `TileSet` occluder layer carries one mask for the whole layer `[UNV]`) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*, pooled at boot to `OCCLUDER_NODE_POOL` (placeholder 240 = `OCCLUDER_POLYS_VIEW_MAX` 120 bound plus 120 hidden out-of-reach; a rebuild that needs more recycles the farthest hidden nodes first and counts `diag.occluder_overflow`, never growing the pool in play), and invents **no geometry**: the polygons are the same rectangles the simulation's segment test uses (EM-20: "one source for collision, light and shadow"); actors and horrors never occlude (ART 3.2). Wall runs merge into one polygon per room edge, door gaps split an edge, each polygon has at most `OCCLUDER_VERTS_MAX` (12) vertices. The invariant: **the union of the merged polygons equals the union of Layout's `OCCLUDES_LIGHT` rectangles exactly** (integer set equality). **The cap `OCCLUDER_POLYS_VIEW_MAX` (120) is keyed to the shadow-reach set, not the in-view set (orchestrator ruling, engine finding F6):** the in-view area is up to 9x at `k_z` 1 on 1080p, 16x on 1440p, 36x on 2160p, and only occluders within `reach_px + OCC_MARGIN_PX` (placeholder 8 px; 48 px if outcome A ships) of an *active shadow-casting light* cost anything; the cap is asserted on that set. **A wall changes the shadow in the same LIGHTING present step that observes it:** when `version(section_id)` bumps for a section that intersects a shadow light's reach disc, its polygons are rebuilt and written in the same LIGHTING present step, in one apply step (a frame is drawn only after the present step returns, so no frame sees a half-written set: none has a missing wall and none has a light shining through one; no second, double-buffered set is kept for an in-reach rebuild, because same-step writes need none and it would be unsized; a light shining through a wall for even one frame is a P1 lie) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*; only sections wholly outside every reach disc are rebuilt within `OCCLUDER_SYNC_BUDGET_US` (placeholder 400, inside the whole Lighting CPU budget `LIGHT_CPU_BUDGET_US`; a synchronous in-reach rebuild is an event frame with its own maximum, LO-29), nearest first. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **Doors:** the door leaf is one sliding rectangle derived by Layout from the Graph's `area` (LY-9: `leaf_w = width_px − floor(width_px × area / area_max)`, flags `SOLID | OCCLUDES_LIGHT | DOOR_LEAF`; the leaf is binary by consequence when `area` jumps between 0 and `area_max`), whose producer is Layout's `layout.doors` hook (LY-10, divisor 1, P3; cited only as the leaf's producer, never as something Lighting orders against), published as a committed rectangle once per tick and never interpolated; the shadow therefore follows the simulation's rectangle, not the door sprite's animation, and may lead or lag the sprite by at most one tick of leaf travel (accepted, since `lit` uses the same rectangle). The `DOOR_LIGHT_OPEN_PM` binary-door threshold named in earlier registry text is retired by LY-9 (a registry supersede, `status: deprecated`, never a silent delete) and is cited only so a reader does not search for it. A door leaf is a Class 2 result valid only after Layout's own `post_restore` (LY-26 c), so Lighting's post-restore rebuild reads leaf rectangles only after that point. -> ADR candidate: tilemap rendering-quadrant size and the occluder merge (whether the engine's `TileMapLayer` merges adjacent occluders is NOT SOURCEABLE; the builder must not depend on it).

# Design Document Rules

- The 8 GDD sections are: Overview, Player Fantasy, Detailed Rules, Formulas, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Tuning Knobs, Acceptance Criteria
- **How many are required depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system **defines numeric rules**: rates, curves, thresholds, costs, damage, drop weights — anything a balance pass would tune) at `standard`, none at `minimal` (the design record there is `design/game-brief.md`). Resolve the tier before flagging a section as missing; see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`
- **The Formulas test is what the system defines, not what it is called.** A system's `Category` in `systems-index.md` is a hint — `Gameplay`, `Economy` and `Progression` almost always qualify — never the test. Do not gate Formulas on a category token: the categories `/map-systems` writes (`Core · Gameplay · Progression · Economy · Persistence · UI · Audio · Narrative · Meta`) do not include `combat` or `AI`, which are example systems *within* `Gameplay`. Every site stating this rule must state the same test.
- **Section-name alias**: The GDD template and `/design-system` author this section as `## Detailed Design`; the design standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. These are the SAME required section — accept either heading and never rewrite one into the other.
- Formulas must include variable definitions, expected value ranges, and example calculations
- Edge cases must explicitly state what happens, not just "handle gracefully"
- Dependencies must be bidirectional — if system A depends on B, B's doc must mention A
- Tuning knobs must specify safe ranges and what gameplay aspect they affect
- Acceptance criteria must be testable — a QA tester must be able to verify pass/fail
- No hand-waving: "the system should feel good" is not a valid specification
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale
- Design documents MUST be written incrementally: create skeleton first, then fill
  each section one at a time with user approval between sections. Write each
  approved section to the file immediately to persist decisions and manage context

# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

160	**Conventions.** Rules are `LO-n` (the prefix is free in every sibling GDD). Formulas are referred to by their registry names (`soft_pool_scale`, `hard_cone_scale`, `modifier_stack`, `flash_governor`, `ambient_value`, `hull_floor`, `shadow_slot_assign`, `cut_order`, `lod_tier`, `per_rung_lit_pixels`, `texture_magnification`, `warmup_ramp`, `glow_threshold_bound`, `light_energy_from_pm`, `gutter_recipe`, `flare_flicker`, `decoy_budget`, `edge_width_screen_px`, `beam_offset`); the Formulas section assigns their `D.n`, and every formula that is not this GDD's is qualified (`EM D.7`, `Graph D.6`, `PIPE D.5`, `PC D.12`, `kernel D.10`). Every engine statement carries `[REF]` (verified from `docs/engine-reference/godot/`), `[BIN]` (existence, type or default only, from the installed 4.7.2 class dump in ART 8.4/8.10) or `[UNV]` (unverified; the named spike step settles it, ART 8.12). Every number this GDD introduces is a placeholder, owner technical-artist, "confirmed by the Lighting spike step n"; every borrowed number is used by its registry name and value and is never restated differently (a needed different value is a CONFLICT surfaced in Open Questions, never a silent change). Rule text is behaviour; where an implementation choice would be needed it is a "-> ADR candidate" note. Zoom-dependent statements hold at **every** rung `k_z` in [1, `k_auto` + 2] and under **both** render passes (PIPE PR-7), on 1080p (`k_auto` 3), 1440p (`k_auto` 4), the Deck (1280x800, `expand`, `k_auto` 2) and 2160p (`k_auto` 6), not only at the default zoom.
161	
162	**LO-1. Rendering only; Lighting reads, the simulation never reads Lighting.** Lighting is a `PRESENTATION` subscriber (KERN:108-113). It reads the last-committed `SIM` views (`emitter.state` and its `shapes()` table, Layout's `OccluderSource`) and, for decoys and module-body glows only, `PERCEPTION_OUT` lists; its notification handlers only mark dirty (kernel CR-10: handler = dirty mark only, writes disabled in handlers) and all drawing happens in the LIGHTING stage's present step of the PresentationDriver (ADR-0009 § 3; stage 6, after AVATAR and FILTER, so the Presenter's beam pose and the decoy list are already written) *(Amended 2026-10-29 — ADR-0009 sync)*. It writes only `CanvasItem`, `Material`, `Light2D`, `LightOccluder2D` and `CanvasModulate` properties, all inside layer 0 of the world viewport that the Pipeline owns. It owns no simulation fact, no reach, no output, no `lit`; it never writes an emitter, never reports a cull to the simulation (a sim-lit but unrendered light would be a P1 lie, so the answer to over-budget is demotion, LO-23, not silence), and registers **no state block, no step hook and no `after:` entry**. Hook ids appear in this document only as things Lighting does *not* order against (`emitter.place`, `body.integrate`) and never in an example. The occluder builder (LO-11) is the one derived-object duty and is classed `PROJECTOR` (KERN:112); the kernel marks that reading provisional pending a technical-director ruling (KERN:117, Open Question 1) and this GDD does not pre-empt it (-> ADR candidate: occluder projector class). The test for ownership (mirroring Emitter State guard G1): if a sentence needs a `Light2D` to be true it belongs here, otherwise it belongs to the owner and is cited by name.
163	
164	**LO-2. The member split, and the one ordering dependency it creates (orchestrator ruling R3, option B).** Lighting writes every *value* member of every light: `enabled`, `energy`, `color`, `texture`, `texture_scale`, `offset`, `shadow_enabled`, `shadow_filter`, `shadow_color`, `shadow_item_cull_mask`, `range_*`, `blend_mode`, `height` (all `[BIN]` existence), and on every builder-owned `LightOccluder2D` the `occluder_light_mask` (LO-24; a per-node property, missing from the earlier write set) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*. Lighting also writes the *pose* members (`position`, `rotation`) of every light **except the local seat's beam**, whose `position` and `rotation` the Avatar Presenter writes from raw aim in the same frame (PC-5: the local beam's `Light2D` rotation, continuous, in the same frame). The Presenter's every other `Light2D` write is forbidden: `enabled`, `energy`, `texture` and `color` are read from `emitter.state` by Lighting, so PC :951 is satisfied vacuously and PC :1062 (the Presenter's `Light2D` writes are exactly `position` and `rotation`) holds as written. The Perception Filter writes **no** `Light2D` member of any kind. The tool layer carries no light, and no `Light2D` is a child of, or positioned by, the tool layer (hands-free chest lamp, LO-28). The beam node's parent is a non-rotating body-frame node, so that a rotated `offset` is never composed with an avatar rotation (lint). Under shadow-origin outcome B (LO-10) the Presenter's `position` write is the **floored foot** (the `body.state` pose, the same floor as the sprite) and Lighting writes `offset` so the texture apex lands on the chest point; under outcome A the Presenter's `position` is the **floored chest point** and `offset` carries only the texture's own apex term, which is non-zero by default because the apex sits at a texture edge (LO-15), so under both outcomes Lighting writes `offset` every render frame. **The ordering dependency, stated:** under outcome B Lighting's `offset` is a function of the rotation the Presenter wrote that same frame (`beam_offset`), so within one render frame the Presenter's pose write precedes Lighting's apply step, always; this is an ordering inside the LIGHTING present step (no hook, no block, no `after:` entry) and is one-directional (the Presenter never reads Lighting). The earlier claim that the two writers "have nothing to race over" remains true, but the dependency is real; if the Presenter's rotation changed after Lighting's `offset` write the apex would be off by up to `|chest − foot| × sin(Δθ)` (1.7 px for PC-5's accepted 2.8 degrees), which the apex-equals-chest lint (≤ 0.01 px every render frame) catches. -> ADR candidate: presentation frame order (a single presentation driver calling Presenter, Lighting, Filter, diagnostics in a fixed order, rather than per-system `process_priority`).
165	
166	**LO-3. Read model, cadence and determinism.** Lighting wakes on the dirty keys `E/<emitter id>` (`(KIND << 32) | id`; fired on create, remove, `switch_on` flip, `shape_id` change, an `output_pm` bucket crossing of `OUTPUT_DIRTY_QUANTUM_PM`, an integer `reach_px` step; pose never dirties; the spill's changes dirty the beam's own key `E/<beam id>`, and on that key Lighting re-polls both the beam's `emitters()` row and `beam_spill(beam_id)`, the spill having no key of its own *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*) and polls pose at render rate. **The `OUTPUT_DIRTY_QUANTUM_PM` bucket is a wake-up granularity, never a value granularity:** every geometry-bearing quantity (`r_lit` read as the published `r_lit_px`, `r_off` read as the published `r_off_px` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*, `texture_scale`, drawn energy) is read or computed from the *exact* `output_pm`, `reach_px` and `r_lit_px` of the last committed tick *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*, re-sampled each render frame for every SOFT light and for any light not in STEADY (reason: `r_lit` and `r_off` are steep at low output; the chain follows the slope `dr/d(output_pm) = R × LIT_ON_PM / output_pm²` (`LIT_OFF_PM` for `r_off`) to within 1 px, about 0.24 px per permille for a 144 px fixture at 300 permille, so a 49-permille lag would be roughly 12 px of edge error, ESTIMATE). Work runs at three cadences: **per committed tick** (a change in the read view's `tick`, observed at the LIGHTING present step): the active set, slot assignment, demotion order, LOD tier, ambient value, occluder sync, using committed inputs only; **per render frame**: pose of moving lights, the modifier chain value, the governor, envelopes, the apply step; **on event**: camera cut, a rung change, a window or pass change, a restore, `LOADING`/`TRANSIT_HOLD` exit, a settings change, the `ALL` dirty collapse (more than `MAX_DIRTY_KEYS` keys). Dirty keys are an optimisation hint only: a full reconcile of every record runs on every event and every `FULL_RECONCILE_TICKS` (placeholder 60), and the incremental result must equal the full result (debug assertion); correctness never depends on a notification arriving. **Determinism, split in two *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*.** (1) *Tick-only decisions* — which emitters are active, slot assignment and lending, demotion order, seat protection, the LOD tier T, the tell tier read, the ambient target, bound or stand-in status — are pure functions of the committed read-view snapshot, the committed camera field, the per-client settings and the previous tick's decision, and are **replay-identical**: a replay and a live run produce identical bindings and identical demotion order. (2) *Envelope and governor outcomes* — the modifier-chain value, the warm-up, cut and shadow fades, gutter onset times, the governor's retiming and every member value that carries them — also depend on `present_time` and the render rate, so they are **deterministic given a recorded frame-time trace** (the `present_time` at every LIGHTING present step), not replay-identical across machines or frame rates. **The plan step / apply step seam and an injectable clock are requirements of this GDD, not ADR candidates:** the plan is computed headlessly, a separate apply step alone names `Light2D`, and the clock is injected so every test supplies its frame-time trace (the testability seam the coding standard asks for). **Fixed pool:** Lighting instantiates a fixed pool of lights, stand-ins, decoy sprites and occluder objects at boot (**`LIGHT_NODE_POOL` = `NONSHADOW_LIGHTS_MAX` 24 + `MAX_FAULT_GLOW` 10 + `LIGHTS_PER_ITEM_MAX` 12 + `SHADOW_SLOTS_MAX` 6 + `n_beam_seats` (the never-demoted `BEAM_SPILL` foot pools, LO-35) = 53 at the single-player MVP and 56 at VS-B**, the non-shadow cap plus the protected excess that may exceed it (fault glows and the seat-protected set, LO-23) plus the shadow casters, asserted at startup against the engine's light and shadow limits read back `[UNV]`; the occluder pool is `OCCLUDER_NODE_POOL`, LO-11) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*; nothing is created or freed during play; a bound emitter keeps its node while eligible (sticky binding, so reordering the demotion list does not rebind lights); every member write is skipped when its value is unchanged (write-on-change). **First observation is never a transition (EP-15):** the first time a light is observed after boot, a restore, a hold exit, a camera cut, a body or pool re-bind, it enters STEADY at its L0 value with no warm-up, no fade and no governor history; warm-up fires only on an observed `output_pm` change from 0 to non-zero between two consecutive committed ticks. **Active set:** an emitter is active iff its reach circle intersects the committed field rectangle expanded by `VIEW_MARGIN_PX` (`VIEW_MARGIN_PX`, placeholder 24 px: the minimum margin is `V_RUN` 3 px per tick × `MAX_TICKS_PER_FRAME` 4 = 12 px of camera travel between committed evaluations, and the placeholder keeps a 2× allowance for camera look-ahead, confirmed at spike step 3, so a light scrolling into view already exists); the test is integer-only so the set is reproducible. A read-view path that does not allocate per poll (struct-of-arrays columns or a caller-provided buffer, plus a monotone `tick` stamp on the view) is asked of Emitter State as Ask E-F (-> ADR candidate), and "newest light" is defined as the **higher emitter id** (ids are monotone, EM-28; Ask E-G confirms), which is reproducible after a restore.

Wall runs merge into one polygon per room edge, door gaps split an edge, each polygon has at most `OCCLUDER_VERTS_MAX` (12) vertices. The `DOOR_LIGHT_OPEN_PM` binary-door threshold named in earlier registry text is retired by LY-9 (a registry supersede, `status: deprecated`, never a silent delete) and is cited only so a reader does not search for it. # Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

content.thinking:
I'm now drafting the LO-11 main rule, replacing the old passage about walls changing shadows to clarify that when a section's version bumps within a shadow light's reach disc, its polygons get rebuilt and written in the same LIGHTING present step, in one apply step.

ignator ordering, not a kernel hook — it runs once per frame after the last tick, so the stage-0 pass observes same-frame bumps before the LIGHTING present step. ADR-0009 chunks PROJECTOR rebuilds but keeps drawing the last complete state until chunking finishes, and crucially polygons for a LightOccluder2D set are only written in one apply at the end of the final chunk, so the engine never sees a half-written set — it's always the old complete set or the new one. In-reach rebuilds are sized to finish within the first chunk (bounded by OCCLUDER_POLYS_VIEW_MAX, 120 polys) so the new set lands in the same stage-0 run before lighting presents.

If the rebuild can't finish in one chunk (weld frame, mass change, ALL), the old set keeps drawing until the final apply, and that lag is explicitly counted as an event frame — I'm treating it as LO-29 rather than inventing a formal diagnostic name. This means light can shine through a new wall for those lag frames, which is an accepted ADR-0009 consequence, not a silent bug, so claiming the system "never lets light through" would be a false statement I should flag. I also want to preserve that there's no second buffered set — the apply writes directly into the same pooled nodes.

done: Blocker 1 (builder placement). LO-1 now says the occluder builder is a separate PROJECTOR registrant at the PROJECT stage (stage 0, ADR-0009 § 1/§ 3), registered after the layout projector and body.projector. It alone creates, frees, reparents and writes polygons for LightOccluder2D. The LIGHTING present step (stage 6) only draws lights and writes the per-node occluder_light_mask.

Blocker 1 (LO-11 wall-change rule). I rewrote the rule to keep the ADR-0009 chunking decision and the no-half-written-set intent together. Chunking bounds the builder's work per frame, not the set the engine sees. Polygons go onto the pooled nodes in one apply at the end of the last chunk of a rebuild, so a rendered frame sees either the last complete set or the new complete set. An in-reach rebuild is sized as a single chunk. The stage-0 run that observes the bump therefore applies it before that frame's LIGHTING present step. If a rebuild cannot fit one chunk (weld frame, ALL collapse), the old set keeps drawing until the final apply, as ADR-0009 says, and the frames in between count as event frames. I chose this over asking for an exemption from chunking, because the ADR is binding and this keeps the design intent.

Blocker 1 (descriptor `after`). LO-11 now says the builder's descriptor names `after` as the layout projector, which is the same-stage presenter order. LO-1, LO-2 and AC-LO-2 now say Lighting registers no kernel `after:` hook-order entry, so the two meanings no longer collide. LO-2 now places the Presenter-pose-before-Lighting ordering across the AVATAR (stage 2) and LIGHTING (stage 6) stages, not inside the present step.

Blocker 1 (other sites). Updated the LO-3 cadence list (the occluder sync runs at stage 0, not in the LIGHTING present step), the S.5 REBUILDING row, the Edge Cases bump entry, AC-LO-1 (creation, freeing and polygon writes only in the stage-0 builder; the mask write in the LIGHTING step), AC-LO-5, and AC-LO-17 (stage-0 apply, plus the rebuild_signature equivalence from ADR-0009 Validation).

Blocker 1 (closed candidate). The PROJECTOR-class ADR candidate is marked closed by ADR-0009 § 1 in LO-1, in the candidates list and in Open Question 5. Open Question 5 now also records the remaining ask to ADR-0009 (see registry_requests).

Blocker 2 (wrong ADR citation). The renderer-and-driver candidate in the candidates list now reads: pinned provisionally to Vulkan by ADR-0008 § 1, reversible at spike steps 1, 2 and 9, and not closed by ADR-0009 § 3, which owns only the PresentationDriver and stage order.
Every changed rule carries a '(Amended 2026-10-29 — sync knock-on fix)' note. No other file was edited.
